timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Everyone has already heard that glaciers are melting catastrophically fast, but have you
heard about how exactly they are melting?
90% of all glaciers on the planet are located in Antarctica, where they are disappearing the fastest.
What is striking is that this is taking place solely in the western part of Antarctica,
whereas in the east, record-breaking cold temperatures are being recorded.
A logical question arises, why is Antarctica melting only on one side?
And the answer is quite simple.
West Antarctica has a totally different geology.
It consists of thin blocks of the Earth's crust that are separated from each other by large tectonic faults,
rich zones.
And in these zones, greater amounts of heat are released.
For example, scientists from Germany and the British Antarctic Survey mapped the geothermal heat flow in West Antarctica,
using data from aeromagnetic observations beneath the Thwaitis Glacier.
They discovered an area where a huge amount of heat comes from the Earth's bowels.
According to scientists, this is due to the fact that the glacier lies in a tectonic trench where the Earth's crust is much thinner.
Surprisingly enough, West Antarctica is one of the largest volcanic regions on Earth.
There are more than 140 volcanoes sleeping under the ice, and they are now much more active than the scientific community previously believed.
A team of researchers from the University of Rhode Island discovered a new factor in the rapid melting of the Pine Island glacier in Antarctica.
It's an earlier unidentified active volcano, buried deep beneath the ice.
The volcanism was indicated by high concentrations of the helium isotope, which comes exclusively from the Earth's mantle.
According to Professor Karen Haywood, geothermal heat from the West Antarctic Rift warms the ocean water.
This in turn leads to the acceleration of ice sheet melting.
Thus, it is the geothermal heat from volcanoes that is contributing to the rapid melting of the Antarctic ice sheet, not global warming at all.
But why? Are there so many volcanoes under the ice of Antarctica?
NASA experts have found out the reason based on data from NASA's ice sat and iceberg satellites.
They have concluded that under the surface of West Antarctica, there is a large mantle plume that is a flow of red hot magma, which rises and expands beneath the Earth's crust.
According to the scientists' calculations, this area is warming with almost the same intensity as the Yellow Zone, Super Volcano.
The heat flux measures 150mW per square meter, reaching 180 in the Rift areas.
This is about three times as much heat as the adjacent rock layers receive.
Thus, all indications are that glaciers in Antarctica are melting, not at all due to anthropogenic factors, but due to the volcanic heat.
At the same time, the temperature of the Earth's crust is rising and parts of the territory are elevating abnormally.
Why does the scientific community ignore the connection between all these phenomena?
Equally intense ice melting is also taking place on another part of the planet in Greenland.
Research conducted in October 2020 showed that Greenland's ice is now melting faster than ever before in the past 12,000 years.
In 2019 alone, Greenland's ice sheet lost the most ice in recorded history, 600 billion tons.
It is also surprising that giant lakes appear under the surface of the glacier, which is actually 1.5 km thick.
As of today, we already know about 6 dozen subglacial lakes of Greenland.
The temperature of the ice surrounding them is around –28 degrees Celsius.
But these lakes do not freeze. Why?
Several research groups of scientists joined in the effort to find an answer to this very question.
They discovered the fact that under Greenland, just as under Antarctica, there is a mantle blue.
Geothermal flows coming from its bowels cause formation of subglacial lakes and melting of glaciers.
Using gravitational research, a team of American scientists led by Professor Ralph Phan Frieza
who founded the thickness of Greenland's crust.
Active melting of glaciers has been observed in the northern part of the island, where the crust is thinner and an increased geothermal flow.
Due to the rising, mantle bloom has been detected.
Using seismic tomography data, scientists from an interdisciplinary team at the Schmidt Institute of Physics of the Earth
flow of magma rises from the center of the core to the Earth's surface right beneath the central part of Greenland.
This is where the largest number of subglacial lakes are located.
The scientists have calculated that theoretical heat flux corresponding to this magma chamber
and found that this heat is sufficient to warm the base of the glacier up to the melting point of the ice.
These same results have been confirmed by similar studies using machine learning technology.
It is obvious that the world's two largest glacial regions, Antarctica and Greenland, are melting because of increased geothermal flows coming from the interior of the planet.
But what is intensifying them?

Mantle plumes have been beneath the glaciers for millions of years, but it is today that their magma rises closer to the Earth's surface and causes increased heating of the Earth's crust from the inside.
This indicates that abnormal processes are starting to occur in the balls of the Earth, and it's very core.
And the main question is, why is it happening precisely now? This answer is simple.
Cyclical changes on a planetary scale occurring every 12,000 years.
The melting of glaciers is only a part of the chain of climatic events that will lead to an imminent catastrophe already in the near future.
